A1.value: Emerging risks for U.S. credit unions

A2.value: VyStar ERM | External research | Updated September 24, 2026 | Outlook: 2029–2031

A5.value: A source-backed external register for ERM analysts to assess, map, link or reject during a later VyStar-specific phase. The workbook does not assess current exposure, controls, owners, residual risk or actual register matches. The seven supplied risk categories are preserved.

A9.value: 34 scenarios across the seven supplied categories. Evidence Type has one dominant value; supporting nuance remains in Assessment Evidence. Broad velocity, qualitative priority and IDs are preserved. Outlook is a forecast of external pressure. Numerical model scores are a separate methodology reference, not VyStar risk exposure.

B13.value: Fraud and payment controls face simultaneous pressure from synthetic impersonation and faster movement across payment rails.

C13.value: Coordinate identity, authentication, payment and recovery monitoring rather than treating each scheme or rail as isolated.

B14.value: Critical-provider concentration is a shared operational vulnerability; AI adds hidden model, cloud and data dependencies to existing core, telecom and payment concentration.

C14.value: Map services through fourth parties, test substitutability and require material-change disclosure.

B15.value: Digital channels compress deposit-outflow velocity even when aggregate system liquidity appears stable.

C15.value: Use intraday scenarios, pre-positioned collateral and same-day escalation authority.

B16.value: Agentic execution, model unreliability and unexplained decisioning can turn an information error into an operational, legal or member-impacting action.

C16.value: Separate agents from chatbots in inventories; constrain authority; validate consequential outputs and adverse-action reasons.

B17.value: Historical insurance cost stress can affect borrower cash flow and collateral. Current Florida rate reductions and insurer entry create important geographic counter-evidence; the net outlook is Unknown.

C17.value: Segment collateral by insurance conditions and test escrow/payment shocks and coverage lapse.

B18.value: CRE refinancing pressure and changed deposit behavior remain uneven but actionable balance-sheet risks.

C18.value: Re-underwrite near maturities and back-test deposit beta, decay and migration assumptions against the latest cycle.

B19.value: Governance and data duties continue to evolve, but developments do not all increase obligations. CFPB withdrew Circular 2023-03; revised bank model guidance excludes GenAI and agentic AI.

C19.value: Maintain a formal horizon scan and reusable governance, consent, data and evidence controls; sequence rule-specific investment by confirmed status.

B20.value: Competition for the member interface is shifting through AI service, embedded finance, open banking and tokenized payments.

C20.value: Track relationship, deposit and channel effects while preserving human access and trusted advice.

B21.value: Workforce capability is both an opportunity and a control-capacity constraint; AI may improve productivity while increasing the need for governance and specialist skills.

C21.value: Build role-specific capability and monitor key-person, vacancy, override and quality indicators without assuming broad displacement.

B22.value: PQC migration, demographic change and AI labor/macro channels warrant monitoring. Their adoption horizons do not establish the event-to-material-impact interval.

C22.value: Use milestone-based monitoring and scenario analysis; do not convert uncertain timelines into false precision.

A25.value: Credit-union-specific incident and adoption evidence remains limited. Fine timing is unvalidated for 20 scenarios; ER-7 has a faster outage pathway than its retained broad band. Outlook is Unknown for 11 risks, including AI labor-to-credit transmission, Florida insurance and several balance-sheet or regulatory pathways. Unknown is not evidence of stability. See Research Gaps and Assessment Evidence.

A30.value: Use Dashboard for the register composition, then filter Emerging Risk Register for the underlying records. Read rationale and source limitations before using an outlook or score. Preserve ER- and S- IDs for LogicGate. Department acceptance, linkage to internal risks, control assessment and rejection remain the next phase.

A2.value: 34 external scenarios | Evidence Type: one dominant value | Outlook: external pressure, 2029–2031 | Updated 2026-09-24

N5.value: Emerging Risk Indicators / Signals to Monitor

D6.value: AI-enabled fraud, deepfakes and synthetic identity attacks

G6.value: Generative AI lowers the cost and increases the realism, scale and personalization of impersonation, account-opening, account-takeover and payment fraud against members and the credit union.

I6.value: Loss arising when synthetic voices, video, documents, identities or conversational agents defeat identity proofing, authentication, employee judgment or member safeguards and cause unauthorized or fraud-induced transactions.

M6.value: Estimated interval: ≤24 hours. T0: a fraudulent payment instruction passes authentication and is accepted for execution. Endpoint: funds leave the account. FinCEN documents immediate withdrawals after deposits. The same-day interval is a transaction-pathway inference, not a measured distribution for all scams. [S-10; S-97] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N6.value: GenAI/deepfake flags in fraud cases; new-account document rejection rate; voice/video authentication exceptions; account takeover and authorized-push-payment losses; member scam complaints; vendor deepfake-detection hit rate; Weak Signal: growth in live multimodal impersonation attempts (S-9–S-11).

O6.value: AI-assisted anomaly detection, behavioral biometrics, document forensics and personalized member education can reduce losses and false positives.

P6.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: remove voice-only authentication; require out-of-band verification for high-risk payments and profile changes; test onboarding and contact-center controls against synthetic media; tag AI-linked fraud cases; refresh member scripts and employee escalation playbooks (S-9, S-10, S-36).

Q6.value: Reinforces ER-2 cyber intrusion, ER-10 data exposure and ER-16 reputation; a stolen identity/data event can seed fraud, while fraud losses and misinformation can accelerate ER-15 liquidity stress.

S6.value: Members may lose savings, vulnerable groups may avoid digital channels, reimbursement disputes may grow, and higher fraud-control friction may reduce inclusion.

T6.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U6.value: Deepfake attribution is inconsistent and many fraud cases would have occurred without AI; layered authentication and provenance controls can reduce exposure (S-29, S-36).

V6.value: Escalate if confirmed AI-assisted fraud loss occurs, voice/video authentication is bypassed, or a critical vendor reports synthetic-media control failure; Judgment-Based Trigger if attempts materially outpace control tuning.

Y6.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Lower-cost impersonation and current financial-fraud reports support growing pressure over 2029–2031. Improved verification may offset losses, so this is a threat forecast rather than a forecast of VyStar losses. [S-9; S-10; S-69]

G7.value: AI is improving attacker productivity in reconnaissance, phishing, vulnerability discovery, malware adaptation and social engineering, shortening the time between exposure and exploitation.

I7.value: Service disruption, data compromise or unauthorized access caused or materially accelerated by AI-enabled offensive techniques against the credit union or its critical providers.

M7.value: Estimated interval: ≤24 hours. T0: successful privileged intrusion into a live environment. Endpoint: unauthorized execution or data access. The July 2026 technical timeline records same-day shell execution and subsequent compromise. Transfer to financial services is an analogy, not an observed VyStar exposure. [S-70; S-71] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N7.value: AI-themed phishing volume; time from vulnerability disclosure to attack attempts; credential-theft alerts; vendor cyber incidents; abnormal automated reconnaissance; AI-related MITRE ATLAS techniques observed; recovery-test results; Weak Signal: autonomous multi-stage intrusion evidence (S-7–S-9, S-31).

O7.value: Defensive AI can improve detection, triage, vulnerability prioritization and incident response, especially where human teams face alert overload.

P7.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: add AI-assisted attack scenarios to cyber exercises; monitor MITRE ATLAS techniques; reduce exposed attack surface; enforce phishing-resistant MFA; validate recovery time for core/member services; require critical vendors to disclose material AI-related cyber incidents (S-4, S-7, S-31).

Q7.value: Reinforces ER-1 fraud, ER-6 vendor failure, ER-7 concentration and ER-10 privacy; simultaneous exploitation of shared technology can create correlated outages.

S7.value: Members can lose service access; employees face higher workload and deception; vendors may propagate common compromise; ecosystem confidence may fall.

T7.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U7.value: Most observed attacker use still augments established tactics rather than creating wholly novel ones; AI also strengthens defense, and exploitation remains constrained by access and operational skill (S-4, S-7).

V7.value: Escalate on confirmed AI-assisted intrusion, material increase in automated attack tempo, exploitation of a shared critical platform, or failure of a recovery objective in an AI-cyber exercise.

Y7.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. NCSC forecasts more effective and accessible AI-assisted intrusions through 2027. Extending that pressure into the 3–5-year horizon is analyst judgment; defensive AI and patching could reduce realized harm. [S-69; S-70]

D8.value: Autonomous AI agent execution and authorization failure

G8.value: Agentic systems can plan and execute multi-step actions through tools and APIs; excessive permissions, prompt injection, memory poisoning or weak human checkpoints can convert a model error into a real transaction or operational change.

I8.value: Unauthorized, incorrect or unsafe business action performed by an AI agent because objectives, permissions, context, tool use, segregation of duties or human oversight are inadequate.

M8.value: Estimated interval: ≤24 hours. T0: an authorized agent accepts a malicious instruction while it has write or execution permissions. Endpoint: unauthorized action or sensitive-data disclosure in that run. This is a technical-pathway inference supported by red-team demonstrations, not a measured CU loss clock. [S-72] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N8.value: Number of agents with write privileges; privileged tool/API calls; human override and rollback events; prompt-injection findings; actions outside approved scope; failed agent simulations; Weak Signal: agents negotiating or initiating financial activity without explicit member confirmation (S-30, S-31).

O8.value: Bounded agents can automate low-risk service, reconciliation, fraud triage and evidence collection while preserving human authority for consequential decisions.

P8.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: inventory agents separately from chatbots; prohibit unbounded payment, lending and access-administration authority; use least privilege, transaction limits, dual approval, immutable logs, sandboxing and tested kill switches; red-team indirect prompt injection before production (S-5, S-30, S-31).

Q8.value: Amplifies ER-4 model failure, ER-5 data poisoning, ER-6 vendor opacity and ER-10 leakage; can turn informational error into direct operational loss.

R8.value: Operational; Model; Cybersecurity; Access Management; Third-Party

S8.value: Employees may be displaced from control loops, members may face irreversible actions, and vendors may become de facto decision makers.

T8.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors

U8.value: Most deployments remain bounded pilots and mature authorization controls can sharply limit consequences; evidence of material financial-institution losses is still sparse.

V8.value: Escalate if any agent can initiate a financial transaction or member-impacting decision without independent approval, or if a red-team test obtains a prohibited tool action.

Y8.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. More agents acting on external content and performing consequential tasks expand the opportunity for authorization failures. Robustness varies across tested models; restricted permissions and approvals can materially contain exposure. [S-72; S-92]

Y20.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Cheaper synthetic persuasion combined with digital withdrawal channels increases the plausible attack surface. This remains a weak-signal forecast; verification, insured balances and liquidity safeguards can contain transmission. [S-10; S-55; S-75]

D21.value: AI-generated misinformation, brand impersonation and trust erosion

G21.value: Synthetic content can impersonate the credit union, executives or members, while unreliable institution-generated AI communications can also undermine confidence.

I21.value: Loss of member or stakeholder trust caused by deceptive or materially inaccurate AI-generated content associated with the credit union or circulating about it.

M21.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: deceptive content reaches members and is believed. Endpoint: material trust loss that changes behavior. Distribution speed alone cannot establish material reputational impact; the reviewed sources do not justify a narrower risk-wide interval. [S-6; S-10] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N21.value: Fake domains/accounts; synthetic brand/executive content; misinformation reach and correction time; AI-generated communication errors; complaint sentiment; media inquiries; content-provenance coverage; Weak Signal: coordinated bot amplification (S-9, S-10, S-29).

O21.value: Verified AI assistants and rapid monitoring can improve member communication, accessibility and misinformation response.

P21.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: monitor brand/executive impersonation; predefine takedown, law-enforcement and member-warning workflows; authenticate official communications; require review for public AI content; rehearse correction within crisis communications; preserve evidence (S-9, S-10, S-29, S-32).

Q21.value: Can trigger ER-1 fraud and ER-15 liquidity; ER-4 hallucinations and ER-10 privacy incidents can create credible reputation events.

R21.value: Reputational; Fraud; Cybersecurity; Liquidity; Compliance / Legal

S21.value: Members may distrust legitimate outreach, employees may face harassment, and misinformation can spread to partners and regulators.

T21.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U21.value: Detection, content credentials and rapid verified communication can limit harm; not all negative synthetic content gains traction, and attribution remains difficult.

V21.value: Escalate on verified synthetic brand/executive content with material reach, member harm, media attention, or measurable abnormal outflows/contact volume.

Y21.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. More realistic impersonation can make verification harder and broaden reputational attacks. Provenance and trusted communication channels may contain damage; the forecast concerns pressure, not demonstrated growing CU reputation losses. [S-10; S-6]

D22.value: Competitive and member-experience gap from insufficient AI adoption

G22.value: Large banks and fintechs can use AI to lower service cost, personalize interactions and speed decisions; under-adoption can weaken relevance, efficiency and member expectations even when avoiding technology risk.

I22.value: Erosion of growth, primacy, efficiency or service quality because the credit union adopts useful AI too slowly, diffusely or without a value-focused portfolio.

M22.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: competitors deploy effective AI while the institution does not. Endpoint: a material operating-efficiency or franchise disadvantage. Early workplace productivity gains do not establish the timing or materiality of a CU competitive gap. [S-99; S-25] Retained Risk Velocity: 13–18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N22.value: AI-enabled service adoption versus peers; cost-to-serve; resolution time; digital abandonment; member satisfaction by channel; pilot-to-production rate; realized benefit versus business case; member demand for AI features (S-2, S-3, S-25).

O22.value: Faster service, fraud prevention, personalized financial guidance, lower costs, accessible interfaces and better risk intelligence.

P22.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: prioritize a small portfolio of governed use cases with measurable member/employee outcomes; establish benefit owners and baseline metrics; scale only after control and value evidence. Near-term: develop reusable data, evaluation and vendor architecture (S-3, S-25).

Q22.value: Tension with ER-8 governance: excessive caution increases strategic risk, while rushed adoption increases ER-3–ER-10. ER-18 capability is a key dependency.

S22.value: Members may migrate to faster providers; employees may maintain costly manual work; vendors may capture more of the member relationship.

T22.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors

U22.value: Many AI programs have uncertain ROI and legacy-system constraints; disciplined later adoption can avoid first-mover failures. Productivity evidence is use-case-specific.

V22.value: Escalate if priority service metrics materially underperform peer/target levels and validated AI use cases remain blocked without a risk-based decision or accountable roadmap.

Y22.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Useful adoption can raise service and cost expectations, increasing pressure on institutions that cannot match it. Benefits vary by task and implementation; the forecast does not imply that adopting every AI tool is strategically beneficial. [S-25; S-3; S-2]

D23.value: Workforce transition, capability and control-capacity failure

G23.value: AI changes task design faster than training, roles and controls adapt; simultaneous skills shortages, shadow use, deskilling, displacement anxiety and loss of human challenge can weaken execution.

I23.value: Failure to maintain the skills, staffing, role clarity, judgment and change capacity needed to adopt and oversee AI while preserving service and controls.

M23.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: AI-driven work change exceeds available trained capacity. Endpoint: a material control or service failure. Staffing enforcement evidence supports the mechanism but not a transferable AI transition-to-impact interval. Short task cycles do not by themselves establish materiality. [S-84; S-25] Retained Risk Velocity: 13–18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N23.value: AI literacy by role; approved-tool adoption; shadow use; rework/error rate; time-to-fill AI/control roles; training completion and demonstrated proficiency; control-owner capacity; engagement/turnover in exposed roles; Weak Signal: loss of entry-level learning pathways.

O23.value: Upskilling existing employees can spread productivity gains, improve retention and preserve institutional knowledge; AI can reduce low-value work.

P23.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: map task-level exposure; define role-based AI competencies; train on verification, data handling and escalation; protect human challenge and entry-level learning; use redeployment before displacement where feasible; selectively recruit scarce assurance/security skills.

Q23.value: Capability constrains ER-3–ER-10 and ER-17; external displacement can become ER-12 credit stress.

R23.value: Strategic; Human Resources; Operational; Model; Conduct

S23.value: Employees may face stress or unequal opportunity; members may lose human access; control teams can become bottlenecks.

U23.value: Broad labor disruption has not yet appeared in aggregate data, and AI may complement rather than replace many roles; capability investment can reduce both displacement and control risk (S-26, S-27).

V23.value: Escalate if material AI use expands faster than role-based competency/control coverage, shadow use rises, critical assurance vacancies persist, or error/rework increases after deployment.

Y23.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Expanding AI use requires new oversight and task-specific skills, making transition execution more demanding. Productivity and training are important offsets; this is not a mass-layoff forecast. [S-3; S-25; S-78]

D24.value: AI financial-agent disintermediation of the member relationship

G24.value: Personal AI agents may increasingly compare, recommend and eventually initiate financial choices across providers, shifting trust and bargaining power from the credit union's channels to external platforms.

I24.value: Loss of member primacy, product visibility or deposits/loans when external AI agents become the main interface for financial search, advice and transaction initiation.

M24.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: members delegate meaningful financial choices to an external agent. Endpoint: material loss of product routing, balances or relationship visibility. Transaction speed is not a sufficient measure of franchise impact; no defensible narrower interval was found. [S-101] Retained Risk Velocity: Over 18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N24.value: Share of traffic/referrals from AI assistants; zero-click product discovery; agent-initiated API activity; member use of external financial copilots; platform access terms; Weak Signal: major platforms launching regulated autonomous finance functions.

O24.value: Trusted, permissioned member agents could deliver personalized financial wellness, proactive savings and easier product navigation.

P24.value: Strategic / 3–5 years: monitor platform and standards development; make products and disclosures machine-readable; test permissioned advisory assistants without transaction authority; protect consent and portability; evaluate whether external agents weaken direct member authentication and loyalty.

Q24.value: Overlaps ER-3 agent authorization, ER-6 platform dependence, ER-9 fairness and ER-17 competitive adoption.

R24.value: Strategic; Member Experience; Third-Party; Data; Reputation

S24.value: Members may receive conflicted recommendations; platforms can steer demand and capture data; smaller institutions may become invisible in agent-mediated comparison.

T24.value: Credit Union; Members; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U24.value: Adoption may be slow because of trust, regulation, liability and integration barriers; members may prefer human or direct digital relationships for consequential decisions.

V24.value: Judgment-Based Trigger: a major consumer platform launches broadly adopted autonomous financial actions, or measurable member acquisition/retention shifts to AI-mediated channels.

Y24.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Agentic services may redirect product discovery and balances, but adoption, authorization, liability and trust are unresolved. Available policy analysis does not establish the net extent or direction of CU relationship loss over 3–5 years. [S-101; S-92]

D25.value: Payment fraud migration across instant and legacy rails

G25.value: Fraud is shifting across checks, ACH, cards and instant payments faster than controls and recovery processes can adapt. Faster settlement compresses intervention time, while criminals continue exploiting legacy rails and member-authorized transfers. [S-39, S-53, S-54, S-65]

I25.value: Risk of member loss, reimbursement expense, operational disruption and control failure as fraud patterns move between payment rails and exploit differences in speed, authentication, liability and recallability. The emerging feature is cross-rail migration and compressed response time—not fraud in general. [S-39, S-53, S-54]

M25.value: Estimated interval: ≤24 hours. T0: a fraudulent instruction reaches a payment rail and bypasses preventive controls. Endpoint: funds settle before intervention. Instant settlement supports a same-day adverse branch; it does not establish that every fraud uses an instant rail or that recovery is impossible. [S-97; S-39] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N25.value: Monthly fraud loss and attempted-loss rate by rail; authorized-push-payment share; check/ACH return and recovery rates; median detection-to-hold time; member scam complaints; new typologies in FinCEN/Fed alerts. [S-53, S-65]

O25.value: Use rail-specific controls, confirmation-of-payee style checks, member friction calibrated by risk, and common fraud taxonomy to improve prevention without broadly slowing payments. [S-53]

P25.value: Immediate: establish one cross-rail fraud dashboard and loss taxonomy; test whether high-risk instant transfers can be paused or stepped up; rehearse recall/recovery with receiving institutions; update member warnings at the point of payment. Near-term: tune limits and authentication using observed loss by rail. [S-39, S-53, S-54]

Q25.value: Reinforces ER-29 (AML), ER-34 (confidence contagion), ER-23 (vendor dependence) and ER-33 (older/member-vulnerability exposure).

S25.value: Member losses and distrust can increase call volumes, complaints and attrition; reimbursement and investigation costs can rise; aggressive friction may reduce digital adoption.

T25.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U25.value: Industry taxonomies and controls are improving, and instant rails can carry richer data. Loss experience may remain concentrated in specific rails or segments rather than system-wide. [S-53, S-54]

V25.value: Escalate if loss rate, attempted-loss rate or unrecovered value breaches an internally approved appetite for any rail; if median detection time exceeds the rail's practical recovery window; or upon a material new typology alert. Judgment-Based Trigger: coordinated fraud campaign targeting credit unions. [S-39, S-65]

Y25.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Faster transfers and complex integrations create more opportunities for fraud to exploit uneven controls. Improved classification and prevention can offset losses, but NCUA identifies growing payment-system risks. [S-39; S-97]

G26.value: Digital banking and networked communications can concentrate withdrawals into hours rather than days. Even when system liquidity is currently moderate, the 2023 bank failures demonstrated that assumptions based on slower depositor behavior can fail abruptly. [S-40, S-55]

I26.value: Risk that deposits migrate or run materially faster than contingency funding, collateral mobilization and decision processes can respond, because members can transfer funds remotely and confidence signals propagate quickly. This is distinct from ordinary deposit competition: the mechanism is speed and concentration of outflow. [S-55]

M26.value: Estimated interval: ≤24 hours. T0: a confidence shock prompts coordinated withdrawal instructions. Endpoint: material liquidity pressure. The SVB chronology establishes a same-day analogue; CU funding structure determines severity and is outside this review. [S-55] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N26.value: Intraday and daily outflows by member/cohort; top depositor concentration; uninsured or operationally mobile balances; digital-transfer limit utilization; collateral pre-positioning time; borrowing test results; social-media/member-contact anomalies. [S-39, S-55, S-56]

O26.value: Faster liquidity telemetry, pre-positioned collateral, segmented member communication and tested digital-service continuity can strengthen resilience and member trust.

P26.value: Immediate: add intraday outflow scenarios to contingency funding tests; measure time-to-cash for each source; pre-position eligible collateral; define same-day liquidity escalation authorities. Near-term: segment runoff assumptions by balance size, product and digital mobility rather than using one average. [S-39, S-55]

Q26.value: Interacts with ER-25 (deposit pricing), ER-34 (confidence contagion), ER-23 (provider outage) and ER-26 (stablecoin substitution).

S26.value: Rapid liquidity use may force high-cost borrowing or asset sales, compress earnings and amplify public concern; defensive rate actions can worsen margin pressure.

T26.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Financial System / Ecosystem

U26.value: Credit-union member affinity, insured balances and cooperative structure may dampen runoff; the Federal Reserve reports aggregate bank funding risks near historical norms. [S-40]

V26.value: Escalate when actual daily/intraday runoff exceeds modeled assumptions for a material segment, when available same-day liquidity falls below the board-approved survival horizon, or when a confidence event produces abnormal digital-transfer activity. [S-39, S-55]

Y26.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Baseline judgment: digitally enabled same-day outflow remains an established structural vulnerability over the horizon. Current NCUA liquidity concerns and the existing withdrawal mechanism support persistence, not a forecast that run frequency will rise. [S-39; S-55]

D27.value: Property-insurance retreat transmitting into household and collateral risk

G27.value: Rising premiums, nonrenewals and coverage gaps can weaken borrower cash flow and collateral protection, especially in catastrophe-exposed markets. The channel is material for a Florida-based credit union even without direct insurance operations. [S-42, S-43]

I27.value: Risk that insurance affordability or availability deterioration raises housing costs, causes lapsed/insufficient coverage, reduces property marketability and increases mortgage, HELOC and small-business credit loss severity. [S-42, S-43]

M27.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: a premium increase or nonrenewal takes effect for a constrained borrower. Endpoint: material repayment or collateral deterioration. Research supports the association, but borrower buffers and payment schedules prevent a defensible universal narrower interval. [S-43] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N27.value: Premium and escrow-payment changes; nonrenewal/forced-place rates; uninsured collateral exceptions; delinquency by hazard zone; insurer exits; catastrophe claims; property values and days-on-market in exposed ZIP codes. [S-42, S-43]

O27.value: Offer proactive escrow counseling, resilience financing and coverage-verification support; incorporate property-level insurance availability into portfolio and member-assistance design.

P27.value: Immediate: stratify real-estate exposure by insurance availability, premium change and catastrophe zone; test payment shock and coverage-lapse scenarios; strengthen renewal monitoring. Near-term: design member outreach before escrow resets and evaluate resilience-improvement lending. [S-42, S-43]

Q27.value: Links to ER-24 (CRE), ER-33 (member vulnerability), ER-21 (liquidity if regional confidence weakens) and operational continuity during disasters.

S27.value: Higher housing expense can reduce disposable income, raise delinquency and consumer-credit stress, depress collateral liquidity and increase forced-place insurance expense.

T27.value: Credit Union; Members; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U27.value: Pricing and availability vary sharply by geography and construction quality; mitigation, state market reforms and insurer re-entry could reduce exposure. [S-42] September 2026 Florida rate reductions and new insurer entry complicate a simple worsening forecast. Net outlook remains Unknown; distinguish local insurance conditions from national history. [S-95; S-96]

V27.value: Escalate when portfolio-weighted premium growth, nonrenewal, forced-place coverage or delinquency in exposed ZIP codes materially exceeds the rest of the portfolio; Judgment-Based Trigger: exit or downgrade of a major regional insurer. [S-42, S-43]

Y27.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. National historical premium stress and borrower-credit findings conflict with current Florida rate reductions and new insurer entry. The net 3–5-year direction depends on geography, catastrophes and capacity; neither nationwide Increasing nor Decreasing is justified. [S-42; S-43; S-95; S-96]

D28.value: Critical provider concentration and low substitutability

G28.value: Credit unions depend on a limited set of core, cloud, telecom, payments and cybersecurity providers. A failure or unilateral change at one provider can affect many services at once, while NCUA's direct examination authority over technology providers remains constrained. [S-52, S-62, S-64]

I28.value: Risk that concentration in a provider or shared subcontractor creates correlated outages, unfavorable contract leverage, delayed recovery or an impractical exit because substitutes are scarce and migration times are long. The risk applies even when VyStar does not directly operate the failed technology. [S-52, S-64]

M28.value: Estimated interval: ≤24 hours. T0: a shared critical provider loses an essential service. Endpoint: dependent transactions or services fail. Visa Europe provides a same-day outage analogue. Replacement lead time measures recovery/substitutability, not velocity to first impact. [S-98; S-79] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N28.value: Critical services by provider/subcontractor; concentration and fourth-party overlap; recovery test results; SLA breaches; unresolved audit findings; exit-time estimates; contract renewal/price changes; provider financial or ownership events. [S-62, S-64]

O28.value: Architecture portability, multi-provider design for truly critical services, shared due diligence and stronger exit clauses can improve resilience and negotiating leverage.

P28.value: Immediate: map critical services through fourth parties and identify single points of failure; validate recovery evidence and communication paths. Near-term: quantify exit time/cost and negotiate data portability, transition assistance and incident-notice rights. Strategic: reduce concentration where practical. [S-62, S-64]

Q28.value: Amplifies ER-20, ER-21, ER-27, ER-31 and ER-34; multiple operational risks may combine into business-continuity and systemic confidence events.

R28.value: Third-Party; Operational; Cybersecurity; Strategic; Compliance / Legal

S28.value: A shared outage can simultaneously interrupt member access, payments and fraud controls; prolonged recovery may cause losses, complaints and liquidity pressure.

T28.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U28.value: Large providers may invest more in resilience than smaller alternatives; diversification can add complexity and does not eliminate common dependencies. [S-64]

V28.value: Escalate if a critical service lacks a tested recovery path, exit estimate or viable substitute; if the same provider/subcontractor supports multiple high-impact services; or upon repeated material SLA failure. [S-62, S-64]

Y28.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Dependence on complex vendor chains can widen correlated operational exposure. NCUA documents third-party vulnerabilities but no systemic CU incident in its reviewed period; the direction is an exposure forecast, not an outage-frequency estimate. [S-79; S-64]

G29.value: Many CRE borrowers must refinance loans originated under lower rates while office demand, operating costs and valuations have changed. Aggregate prices have shown stabilization, but maturity and property-type dispersion keep loss risk uneven. [S-40, S-41, S-68]

I29.value: Risk that refinancing at higher debt service, weaker occupancy or lower collateral values makes otherwise performing CRE exposures unable to refinance or repay, particularly where local deposit growth and CRE concentration are linked. [S-41]

M29.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: refinancing fails or adverse terms become effective at maturity. Endpoint: material repayment deterioration or credit loss. Market reports establish vulnerability but not a universal trigger-to-material-impact interval across loan structures and workouts. [S-40] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N29.value: Maturities by quarter; debt-service coverage at stressed rates; LTV using current valuations; occupancy/lease rollover; borrower liquidity; criticized/classified trends; extensions and modifications; property-type/geographic concentration. [S-40, S-41]

O29.value: Early borrower engagement, selective refinance structures and disciplined financing of adaptive reuse or resilient properties can protect relationships and improve portfolio mix.

P29.value: Immediate: create a 24-month maturity map and re-underwrite material exposures using current rents, expenses, cap rates and refinance rates; identify borrowers dependent on sale/refinance. Near-term: set property-type watch lists and workout capacity. [S-40, S-41]

Q29.value: Connects to ER-22 (insurance), ER-25 (rate regime), local deposit conditions and broader household/employer stress.

S29.value: Extensions can delay loss recognition and tie up capital; property weakness can reduce local employment, member income and deposit growth.

T29.value: Credit Union; Members; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U29.value: The Fed reports aggregate CRE price stabilization and vulnerabilities are concentrated rather than universal. Strong sponsors and low leverage may absorb refinancing shocks. [S-40]

V29.value: Escalate when stressed DSCR or LTV breaches internal underwriting thresholds, when a material maturity lacks a credible takeout 12 months ahead, or when occupancy/valuation declines invalidate the base case. [S-40, S-41]

Y29.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Price stabilization and loan modifications mitigate stress, while upcoming maturities and structural-use differences sustain vulnerability. These mixed signals do not establish a common 2029–2031 direction across property types and locations. [S-40; S-41]

D30.value: Structural deposit-pricing and repricing-model regime shift

G30.value: Higher funding costs, product transparency and uneven asset/liability repricing challenge deposit-beta and decay assumptions calibrated to older cycles. NCUA notes that loans and funding costs have not repriced uniformly and continues to prioritize IRR. [S-39, S-56]

I30.value: Risk that deposit rates, balances and member migration respond differently from historical model assumptions, causing margin compression or duration mismatch under both rising and falling rates. This is an assumption-regime risk, not generic rate volatility. [S-39]

M30.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: deposit migration or repricing departs from ALM assumptions. Endpoint: material funding-cost or margin deterioration. Pricing cycles do not by themselves establish when the effect becomes material. [S-39; S-40] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N30.value: Deposit beta by product/cohort; migration from nonmaturity to term/high-yield products; exception pricing; decay and attrition; margin sensitivity; EVE/NEV and NII scenarios; wholesale funding use; model back-testing variance. [S-39, S-56]

O30.value: Cohort-level pricing analytics and relationship-based products can retain stable funding while avoiding blanket rate increases.

P30.value: Immediate: back-test deposit beta, decay and migration assumptions against the latest rate cycle; add asymmetric up/down scenarios and member-cohort behavior. Near-term: link pricing authority to liquidity value and relationship economics. [S-39]

Q30.value: Reinforces ER-21 (outflow speed), ER-26 (stablecoin substitution) and ER-24 (CRE refinance); margin pressure can constrain investment in controls and member service.

S30.value: Unexpected funding cost or duration can reduce earnings and capital accumulation, prompting pricing or growth actions that alter competitive position.

U30.value: Recent rate declines have eased some pressure, and member relationships may produce more stable behavior than market-rate accounts. [S-39]

V30.value: Escalate if actual beta, decay or product migration materially exceeds model assumptions for two reporting periods, or if combined NII/EVE sensitivity breaches board limits under plausible scenarios. [S-39]

Y30.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Funding costs and incomplete repricing remain concerns, but NCUA also identifies easing pressures. Future rate paths and member elasticity are unresolved, so a net 3–5-year direction is not defensible. [S-39; S-40]

G31.value: The GENIUS Act created a federal payment-stablecoin framework, lowering a major adoption barrier. If stablecoins become routine payment or treasury instruments, some transaction balances and payment economics could move outside credit-union accounts. [S-44, S-45, S-66]

I31.value: Risk that regulated stablecoins or tokenized deposits shift member balances, transaction data and payment relationships to issuers, wallets or platforms outside the credit union, reducing low-cost funding and fee opportunities. [S-44, S-45]

M31.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: members shift meaningful activity to tokenized deposits or stablecoins. Endpoint: net loss of stable funding or payment franchise. Settlement can be instant, but recycling through reserve deposits and adoption scale determine material impact. No defensible risk-wide narrower interval. [S-45; S-66] Retained Risk Velocity: 13–18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N31.value: Stablecoin market/payment volume; member transfers to exchanges/wallets; merchant and payroll adoption; issuer partnerships; implementing rules; stablecoin-related deposit flows; competitor product launches. [S-44, S-45]

O31.value: Evaluate compliant wallet, settlement or member-education partnerships; use tokenization to improve payments while preserving insured-account relationships. [S-66]

P31.value: Immediate: assign ownership and map funding/payment revenue at risk; monitor implementation rules and member flows. Near-term: define partnership guardrails and test one low-risk use case only if member demand and legal authority are clear. [S-44, S-66]

Q31.value: Links to ER-21, ER-25, ER-29 and ER-30; provider/platform concentration could amplify ER-23.

R31.value: Strategic; Liquidity; Payments; Compliance / Legal; Third-Party

S31.value: Deposit substitution may raise funding cost; loss of transaction data can weaken relationship economics; new rails may also lower cross-border or settlement cost.

T31.value: Credit Union; Members; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U31.value: Stablecoins remain a small share of household payments, adoption forecasts vary, and insured deposits retain legal and trust advantages. [S-45]

V31.value: Escalate if member outflows to stablecoin platforms become material, a major payroll/merchant network adopts stablecoin settlement, or implementing rules enable direct credit-union issuance/participation. Judgment-Based Trigger. [S-44]

Y31.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Commercial development and tokenized-payment alternatives are likely to increase competitive pressure. Reserve design may recycle funding to banks, and CUs can participate in new services; the forecast is pressure, not inevitable net deposit flight. [S-66; S-45; S-44]

D32.value: Open-banking rule reset and data-portability execution risk

G32.value: CFPB finalized Section 1033 data-access requirements in 2024, then formally reopened key issues in 2025, including fees, representatives, security and privacy. The direction toward consumer-directed data access remains, but implementation obligations and timing are unsettled. [S-46, S-47]

I32.value: Risk of misallocated investment, compliance gaps, data leakage or competitive disadvantage as the legal and technical requirements for consumer-authorized financial data sharing are revised. [S-46, S-47]

M32.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: a confirmed rule or court action invalidates a committed data-portability design. Endpoint: material rework cost or applicable noncompliance. The stay does not establish project costs or a new compliance clock, so a finer interval would be speculative. [S-81; S-46] Retained Risk Velocity: 13–18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N32.value: CFPB notices/final rule; court orders; recognized standards; API adoption; screen-scraping volume; third-party data incidents; implementation spend; member data-sharing demand. [S-46, S-47]

O32.value: Secure APIs can reduce credential sharing, improve member control and support new aggregation/advice services.

P32.value: Immediate: preserve reusable API, consent and third-party-control work while separating it from rule-specific requirements; inventory scraping exposure. Near-term: scenario-plan at least two rule outcomes and maintain traceable decisions. [S-46, S-47]

Q32.value: Interacts with ER-23 (providers), ER-28 (privacy), ER-30 (platform competition) and ER-20 (fraud).

R32.value: Compliance / Legal; Data; Cybersecurity; Third-Party; Strategic

S32.value: Premature or delayed investment can waste resources; weak consent or interface controls may create fraud, privacy and liability exposure.

T32.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U32.value: A revised rule could reduce cost or security concerns; litigation and agency policy can materially change timing. [S-46, S-47]

V32.value: Escalate upon a proposed/final revised rule, court action changing enforceability, recognition of a governing standard, or evidence that scraping/API traffic creates material security or member-service issues. [S-46, S-47]

Y32.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Litigation and reconsideration can delay, narrow or redirect implementation duties. The net 3–5-year burden and timing remain unsettled; continued uncertainty does not justify a directional Increasing classification. [S-81; S-46; S-47]

D33.value: Fragmented state privacy and data-security obligations

G33.value: States continue enacting differing privacy, data-broker, biometric and security requirements. Financial-sector exemptions are not uniform, so GLBA coverage does not automatically eliminate all state-law exposure. [S-48, S-49]

I33.value: Risk that a patchwork of state requirements creates inconsistent rights, notices, retention rules, vendor obligations and incident duties across members and business activities, increasing legal and operating error. [S-48, S-49]

M33.value: Estimated interval: >30–90 days. T0: a valid rights request starts an applicable response clock in a process with incorrect state-law mapping. Endpoint: a missed legal response duty. Virginia provides a 45-day example, subject to extensions; GLBA exemptions must be tested first. This conditional analogue is not a VyStar applicability conclusion or time to penalties. [S-102; S-83] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N33.value: New laws/effective dates; applicability by entity/data exemption; privacy requests by state; vendor-contract gaps; retention exceptions; complaints/enforcement; conflicting legal interpretations. [S-48, S-49]

O33.value: A common high-standard privacy control set can simplify operations and differentiate the member trust proposition.

P33.value: Immediate: maintain a state applicability matrix at the activity/data level, not only entity level; map rights to one intake workflow; update vendor clauses and retention controls. Near-term: adopt a common control baseline with documented exceptions. [S-48, S-49]

Q33.value: Links to ER-27, ER-23, ER-20 and ER-34; privacy incidents can become reputation and fraud events.

R33.value: Compliance / Legal; Privacy; Data; Third-Party; Reputational

S33.value: Duplicated processes and inconsistent responses raise cost and enforcement risk; over-deletion or over-retention can impair fraud, legal and member-service needs.

T33.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors

U33.value: Many laws exempt GLBA-regulated data or institutions in part; scope must be assessed activity by activity and may be narrower than headline counts imply. [S-48, S-49]

V33.value: Escalate when a new law covers a material member population/activity without an operational owner, or when exemption interpretation changes, enforcement begins, or request volumes exceed capacity. [S-48, S-49]

Y33.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Continued state-by-state development can increase applicability and mapping complexity. GLBA exemptions and differences in covered entities may reduce direct CU obligations; this forecasts fragmentation pressure, not a count of new binding laws. [S-82; S-83; S-49]

D34.value: Illicit-finance controls lagging faster and digital-value movement

G34.value: Instant payment availability and regulated stablecoin growth increase the speed and variety of value movement. AML, sanctions, scam and case-management processes built around slower settlement may not intervene in time. [S-39, S-44, S-54, S-65]

I34.value: Risk that transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, escalation and reporting do not adapt to faster settlement and digital-asset counterparties, producing undetected illicit activity, late holds or poor SAR decision evidence. [S-39, S-65]

M34.value: Estimated interval: ≤24 hours. T0: an illicit payment passes deficient monitoring or hold controls. Endpoint: funds move before prevention or detection. This is a transaction-speed inference supported by instant settlement and a documented monitoring-failure analogue; enforcement consequences may occur much later. [S-97; S-84] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N34.value: Alert latency versus settlement; digital-asset counterparties; sanctions false-negative testing; SAR themes; scam-to-AML referrals; 314(b) use; transaction-monitoring backlog; typology coverage. [S-65]

O34.value: Richer payment data, shared typologies and real-time risk scoring can improve detection and reduce low-value alerts.

P34.value: Immediate: compare screening/monitoring latency with each rail's settlement speed; connect fraud and AML cases; update typology coverage for wallets, stablecoins and investment scams. Near-term: test real-time interdiction and evidence retention. [S-53, S-65]

Q34.value: Strongly connected to ER-20, ER-26, ER-27 and ER-23.

R34.value: BSA / AML; Sanctions; Compliance / Legal; Fraud; Operational

S34.value: Control lag can produce member loss, enforcement exposure and correspondent/payment restrictions; excessive blocking can harm access and trust.

T34.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U34.value: Stablecoin regulation and richer ISO 20022 data may improve transparency; adoption pace and actual illicit-use patterns remain uncertain. [S-44, S-54]

V34.value: Escalate if high-risk payments settle before screening disposition, monitoring backlog exceeds approved service levels, a new typology is not covered, or regulators issue material digital-asset/instant-payment guidance. [S-39, S-65]

Y34.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Faster and more diverse value-transfer channels increase adaptation demands on AML controls. Risk-based modernization and better analytics may contain the gap; the direction is conditional external pressure, not a prediction of violations. [S-39; S-66; S-84]

D35.value: Embedded-finance erosion of the member interface

G35.value: Financial products are increasingly distributed inside merchant, payroll and technology platforms. The credit union may retain an account or loan while losing the daily interface, transaction data and cross-sell relationship. [S-46, S-66, S-67]

I35.value: Risk that third-party platforms become the primary member experience and decision layer, commoditizing the credit union's balance sheet and weakening loyalty, data access and product discovery.

M35.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: a platform takes over material customer-facing discovery and routing. Endpoint: sustained loss of relationship visibility or product economics. Daily transaction routing is not equivalent to material franchise loss; no transferable narrower lag was found. [S-85] Retained Risk Velocity: 13–18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N35.value: Share of acquisition/transactions through third parties; active digital users; direct-deposit primacy; product-per-member; wallet/default-payment status; API traffic; platform referral economics; attrition after aggregator use.

O35.value: Embed VyStar services selectively in member journeys while preserving consent, brand, servicing rights and relationship data; improve direct digital experience in high-frequency needs.

P35.value: Near-term: identify the member journeys where VyStar is losing interface primacy; set partnership principles for brand, data, complaint ownership and exit. Test relationship economics before scaling. [S-46, S-67]

Q35.value: Connects to ER-26, ER-27, ER-23, ER-25 and ER-33.

S35.value: Lower engagement can reduce cross-sell, pricing power and low-cost deposits; platform dependence can transfer complaint and conduct risk back to the credit union.

T35.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors

U35.value: Members may prefer trusted direct relationships for complex decisions; partnerships can expand reach rather than displace it if economics and data rights are controlled.

V35.value: Escalate if direct-deposit primacy, active digital engagement or products-per-member deteriorate in segments using third-party financial platforms, or if a major platform changes access/fees. Judgment-Based Trigger.

Y35.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Platforms that control discovery and distribution can weaken the direct member interface as embedded services develop. Partnerships may also extend CU reach; a directional pressure forecast does not assume inevitable disintermediation. [S-85; S-66]

G36.value: NIST finalized initial post-quantum standards and urges migration because integration takes time. The nearer risk is not a proven cryptographically relevant quantum computer; it is failing to inventory and replace vulnerable cryptography across long-lived systems and vendors before deadlines or exposure. [S-50, S-51]

I36.value: Risk that legacy encryption, signatures or certificates remain in production or archived data after quantum-vulnerable algorithms become unacceptable, creating confidentiality, authentication, availability and compliance exposure. [S-50, S-51]

M36.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: a cryptographic dependency becomes unsafe or unacceptable while migration remains incomplete. Endpoint: material confidentiality, authentication or interoperability failure. Neither a planning deadline nor years until quantum capability provides the trigger-to-impact interval. [S-100; S-86] Retained Risk Velocity: Over 18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N36.value: Cryptographic inventory coverage; vendor PQC roadmaps; certificate/algorithm use; data confidentiality life; migration milestones; crypto-agility test results; NIST/CISA deadlines; unsupported devices. [S-50, S-51]

O36.value: Crypto-agility can reduce future migration cost and improve certificate/key governance now.

P36.value: Immediate: assign ownership and inventory cryptography in critical applications, interfaces, archives and vendor services. Near-term: require vendor roadmaps and prioritize long-lived confidential data. Strategic: test hybrid/PQC implementations and retirement plans. [S-50, S-51]

Q36.value: Depends on ER-23 provider visibility; failure can amplify privacy, fraud and systemic service risks.

R36.value: Cybersecurity; Operational; Third-Party; Data; Compliance / Legal

S36.value: Late migration may require emergency system changes, create service incompatibility or expose historical member data and transaction integrity.

T36.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U36.value: No cryptographically relevant quantum computer is known today; timelines differ widely and standards may evolve. Migration itself can introduce performance or interoperability defects. [S-50]

V36.value: Escalate if a critical system lacks a cryptographic inventory/vendor plan, NIST/CISA changes transition guidance, or a credible breakthrough materially advances the threat timeline. Judgment-Based Trigger. [S-50, S-51]

Y36.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Migration workload and dependency coordination become more pressing as organizations replace vulnerable cryptography. Available standards mitigate risk; Increasing reflects transition pressure, not a prediction of quantum compromise within 3–5 years. [S-100; S-86; S-50]

G37.value: Demand for cybersecurity and financial-control skills is growing while many openings reflect replacement needs. Credit unions compete with banks, technology firms and vendors for scarce expertise, creating key-person and assurance bottlenecks. [S-58, S-59]

I37.value: Risk that insufficient depth in cybersecurity, compliance, model, fraud, treasury and vendor oversight slows change, weakens challenge and concentrates critical knowledge in too few people. The emerging mechanism is simultaneous growth in specialized control demand and replacement pressure. [S-58, S-59]

M37.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: a key specialist leaves or required control workload exceeds available capacity. Endpoint: a material missed review or control failure. Replacement capacity and task schedules govern the lag; employment projections and a staffing-enforcement case do not establish a universal interval. [S-58; S-59; S-84] Retained Risk Velocity: 13–18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N37.value: Time-to-fill and offer acceptance; regretted turnover; single-incumbent critical roles; control backlog; overdue validation/audit issues; contractor dependence; training/certification coverage; succession readiness.

O37.value: Build internal career paths, rotations and shared capabilities; automate low-value work; use selective managed services without outsourcing accountability.

P37.value: Immediate: map critical roles to named backups and workload; identify control processes dependent on one person. Near-term: create targeted development/rotation plans and retention measures; set limits on contractor concentration. [S-58, S-59]

Q37.value: Capacity constraints amplify ER-20, ER-23, ER-27, ER-29 and ER-31 and can slow opportunity execution under ER-26/ER-30.

R37.value: Strategic; Operational; Human Capital; Compliance / Legal

S37.value: Backlogs and weak succession can increase control failures, vendor dependence and change cost; sustained overload may raise turnover further.

U37.value: National occupation forecasts do not measure VyStar's local labor pool; remote work, training and managed services may expand supply. [S-58, S-59]

V37.value: Escalate when a critical role lacks a ready backup, vacancy/backlog exceeds approved tolerance, or turnover affects multiple linked control functions. Judgment-Based Trigger.

Y37.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Projected security-specialist demand supports continued hiring pressure, while compliance employment grows more modestly. Supply, automation and retention can offset this; the forecast does not treat job openings as a measured skill shortage. [S-58; S-59]

G38.value: The U.S. older population is growing while access gaps persist for lower-income, disabled and minority households. A uniform digital-first or branch-heavy model can fail both high-digital and assisted-service segments. [S-60, S-61, S-67]

I38.value: Risk that diverging member needs by age, disability, income, language and digital confidence make one channel model economically or operationally unsustainable, weakening access, growth and member trust. [S-60, S-67]

M38.value: Estimated interval: Unknown. Insufficient evidence to refine the interval. T0: a channel change removes a usable service option for an affected segment. Endpoint: material access or relationship harm. Demographic trends do not supply a change-to-impact clock, and no transferable CU interval was found. [S-60; S-88] Retained Risk Velocity: Over 18 months. The retained band is not newly validated by this timing review.

N38.value: Channel use and cost-to-serve by segment; abandonment; accessibility complaints; branch traffic/appointments; call reasons; digital enrollment and failure; proxy/caregiver needs; fraud loss by age; underserved access gaps. [S-60, S-67]

O38.value: Design accessible hybrid service, caregiver/proxy controls, multilingual support and segment-specific financial-health tools.

P38.value: Near-term: segment channel journeys and failure points; incorporate accessibility and assisted-service demand into branch/digital plans. Strategic: test hybrid formats before irreversible footprint changes. [S-60, S-67]

Q38.value: Connects to ER-20 (scams), ER-30 (interface), ER-32 (workforce) and ER-34 (trust).

S38.value: Poor fit can increase fraud vulnerability, exclusion, complaints and attrition; overbuilding either channel raises cost and reduces investment flexibility.

U38.value: Age does not determine digital preference; local member composition may differ from national projections. Segment behavior must be measured rather than inferred. [S-60, S-67]

V38.value: Escalate if abandonment, complaints, losses or attrition diverge materially by member segment/channel, or if a footprint decision would remove the only practical access mode for a material population. Judgment-Based Trigger.

Y38.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Aging and heterogeneous access needs are likely to make inclusive channel design more demanding. Digital familiarity and accessible alternatives can reduce exclusion; the forecast concerns segmentation pressure, not deterioration for every older member. [S-60; S-61; S-88]

D39.value: Networked confidence shock and reputation-to-liquidity contagion

G39.value: The 2023 failures showed that networked communication can accelerate collective depositor action. For credit unions, a localized service, fraud or governance event could spread beyond the original facts and become a liquidity or member-contact event before normal communications cycles respond. [S-55]

I39.value: Risk that fast, networked claims—accurate or inaccurate—trigger concentrated member concern, withdrawals, complaints or employee disruption, converting a reputation event into operational and liquidity stress. [S-55]

M39.value: Estimated interval: ≤24 hours. T0: a credible networked confidence shock reaches a responsive depositor group. Endpoint: behavior changes and liquidity pressure. The SVB chronology provides a same-day analogue; transfer depends on depositor structure and is not an internal exposure assessment. [S-55] Retained Risk Velocity: 0–12 months. Estimate applies only to this specified branch, not every possible outcome.

N39.value: Abnormal contact-center and complaint volume; social/media mention velocity and source credibility; digital transfer attempts; service-status traffic; misinformation themes; employee/member sentiment; correction reach.

O39.value: Pre-approved fact-based communications, transparent incident status and trusted community voices can strengthen confidence during real events.

P39.value: Immediate: integrate communications, liquidity, fraud and operations into one confidence-event playbook; pre-authorize facts, spokespeople and escalation channels; exercise a weekend scenario. [S-55]

Q39.value: Can be triggered by ER-20, ER-21, ER-23 or ER-28 and then amplify ER-21. It is a cross-category cascade rather than a substitute for the underlying event.

S39.value: Even a short-lived claim can create withdrawals, call surges, employee distraction and long-lived trust loss; overreaction may amplify the claim.

T39.value: Credit Union; Members; Employees; Third-Party Vendors; Financial System / Ecosystem

U39.value: NCUA removed reputation risk as a standalone supervisory risk in 2025; this row is retained for ERM because the observable consequence pathway is confidence-to-liquidity, not because adverse publicity alone is a safety-and-soundness category. [S-63]

V39.value: Judgment-Based Trigger: a high-velocity claim from a credible or widely amplified source coincides with abnormal member contacts, digital transfers or service-status traffic; escalate immediately when two channels corroborate the signal. [S-55, S-63]

Y39.value: Analyst outlook, 2026-09-24; horizon 2029–2031. Baseline judgment: networked confidence transmission remains a persistent vulnerability. Documented run mechanisms and operational-confidence channels support continued relevance, but not a defensible rising frequency forecast. Communication and funding resilience can limit spread. [S-55; S-89]

columns.name: Emerging Risk Indicators / Signals to Monitor

A2.value: Selected using Evidence Strength, Risk Velocity and current action relevance; this is not a likelihood/impact score

C6.value: AI-enabled fraud, deepfakes and synthetic identity attacks

G6.value: Generative AI lowers the cost and increases the realism, scale and personalization of impersonation, account-opening, account-takeover and payment fraud against members and the credit union. Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H6.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: remove voice-only authentication; require out-of-band verification for high-risk payments and profile changes; test onboarding and contact-center controls against synthetic media; tag AI-linked fraud cases; refresh member scripts and employee escalation playbooks (S-9, S-10, S-36).

C7.value: Payment fraud migration across instant and legacy rails

G7.value: Fraud is shifting across checks, ACH, cards and instant payments faster than controls and recovery processes can adapt. Faster settlement compresses intervention time, while criminals continue exploiting legacy rails and member-authorized transfers. [S-39, S-53, S-54, S-65] Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H7.value: Immediate: establish one cross-rail fraud dashboard and loss taxonomy; test whether high-risk instant transfers can be paused or stepped up; rehearse recall/recovery with receiving institutions; update member warnings at the point of payment. Near-term: tune limits and authentication using observed loss by rail. [S-39, S-53, S-54]

G8.value: AI is improving attacker productivity in reconnaissance, phishing, vulnerability discovery, malware adaptation and social engineering, shortening the time between exposure and exploitation. Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H8.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: add AI-assisted attack scenarios to cyber exercises; monitor MITRE ATLAS techniques; reduce exposed attack surface; enforce phishing-resistant MFA; validate recovery time for core/member services; require critical vendors to disclose material AI-related cyber incidents (S-4, S-7, S-31).

G9.value: Digital banking and networked communications can concentrate withdrawals into hours rather than days. Even when system liquidity is currently moderate, the 2023 bank failures demonstrated that assumptions based on slower depositor behavior can fail abruptly. [S-40, S-55] Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H9.value: Immediate: add intraday outflow scenarios to contingency funding tests; measure time-to-cash for each source; pre-position eligible collateral; define same-day liquidity escalation authorities. Near-term: segment runoff assumptions by balance size, product and digital mobility rather than using one average. [S-39, S-55]

C10.value: Property-insurance retreat transmitting into household and collateral risk

G10.value: Rising premiums, nonrenewals and coverage gaps can weaken borrower cash flow and collateral protection, especially in catastrophe-exposed markets. The channel is material for a Florida-based credit union even without direct insurance operations. [S-42, S-43] Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H10.value: Immediate: stratify real-estate exposure by insurance availability, premium change and catastrophe zone; test payment shock and coverage-lapse scenarios; strengthen renewal monitoring. Near-term: design member outreach before escrow resets and evaluate resilience-improvement lending. [S-42, S-43]

C11.value: Critical provider concentration and low substitutability

G11.value: Credit unions depend on a limited set of core, cloud, telecom, payments and cybersecurity providers. A failure or unilateral change at one provider can affect many services at once, while NCUA's direct examination authority over technology providers remains constrained. [S-52, S-62, S-64] Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H11.value: Immediate: map critical services through fourth parties and identify single points of failure; validate recovery evidence and communication paths. Near-term: quantify exit time/cost and negotiate data portability, transition assistance and incident-notice rights. Strategic: reduce concentration where practical. [S-62, S-64]

G12.value: Many CRE borrowers must refinance loans originated under lower rates while office demand, operating costs and valuations have changed. Aggregate prices have shown stabilization, but maturity and property-type dispersion keep loss risk uneven. [S-40, S-41, S-68] Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H12.value: Immediate: create a 24-month maturity map and re-underwrite material exposures using current rents, expenses, cap rates and refinance rates; identify borrowers dependent on sale/refinance. Near-term: set property-type watch lists and workout capacity. [S-40, S-41]

C13.value: Structural deposit-pricing and repricing-model regime shift

G13.value: Higher funding costs, product transparency and uneven asset/liability repricing challenge deposit-beta and decay assumptions calibrated to older cycles. NCUA notes that loans and funding costs have not repriced uniformly and continues to prioritize IRR. [S-39, S-56] Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H13.value: Immediate: back-test deposit beta, decay and migration assumptions against the latest rate cycle; add asymmetric up/down scenarios and member-cohort behavior. Near-term: link pricing authority to liquidity value and relationship economics. [S-39]

C14.value: AI model unreliability, drift and validation failure

G14.value: AI outputs can be inaccurate, unstable, overconfident or sensitive to changing data and prompts; traditional validation may not cover foundation models, continuous updates or generative behavior. Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H14.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: create a risk-tiered AI/model inventory; define intended use and prohibited reliance; validate against representative and edge-case data; monitor drift and vendor version changes; require human verification of member, legal, financial and risk conclusions (S-2, S-5, S-14).

C15.value: Third-party hidden AI and outsourced control failure

G15.value: Vendors may embed, change or subcontract AI without sufficient transparency, while the credit union remains accountable for service, compliance, security and member outcomes. Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H15.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: add AI disclosure to procurement and annual reviews; require data-use limits, update notice, testing evidence, audit/access rights, incident notification, subcontractor transparency, exit support and manual fallback; map fourth-party model/cloud dependencies (S-2–S-4, S-17).

G16.value: AI-specific frameworks and supervisory expectations are developing while existing consumer, privacy, security and safety obligations already apply, creating governance and change-management risk even without a single comprehensive U.S. AI law. Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H16.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: establish accountable AI governance; maintain use-case/model/vendor inventory; risk-tier uses; map existing laws and the Treasury FS AI RMF to controls; monitor formal federal and relevant state developments; retain approval, testing and decision records (S-1–S-3, S-5).

C17.value: Algorithmic discrimination and unexplainable member decisions

G17.value: AI decisioning can reproduce proxy discrimination or produce reasons that do not match actual model behavior; fair-lending and adverse-action duties apply regardless of technical complexity. Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H17.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: prohibit deployment where adverse-action reasons cannot be validated; test outcomes and error rates across protected/proxy groups; review marketing, fraud and collections as well as lending; provide appeal and human-review paths; require vendor-level evidence (S-12–S-14).

C18.value: Member-data privacy, confidentiality and proprietary-data leakage

G18.value: Prompts, training, retrieval, logs and vendor telemetry can expose nonpublic personal information, authentication data, employee information or proprietary material beyond approved purposes and jurisdictions. Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H18.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: deploy approved tools with enterprise data terms; block sensitive data in unapproved services; map prompts, retrieval, logs and subprocessors; enforce least privilege, retention and deletion; test inference and extraction; train employees on prohibited data (S-6, S-8).

C19.value: AI-generated misinformation, brand impersonation and trust erosion

G19.value: Synthetic content can impersonate the credit union, executives or members, while unreliable institution-generated AI communications can also undermine confidence. Evidence: High; velocity: 0–12 months.

H19.value: Immediate / 0–12 months: monitor brand/executive impersonation; predefine takedown, law-enforcement and member-warning workflows; authenticate official communications; require review for public AI content; rehearse correction within crisis communications; preserve evidence (S-9, S-10, S-29, S-32).

C20.value: Autonomous AI agent execution and authorization failure

G20.value: Agentic systems can plan and execute multi-step actions through tools and APIs; excessive permissions, prompt injection, memory poisoning or weak human checkpoints can convert a model error into a real transaction or operational change. Evidence: Medium; velocity: 0–12 months.
